newsitem.title: GERMANY: German govt eyes higher VAT, pension taxes.
newsitem.headline: German govt eyes higher VAT, pension taxes.

text.p: German Finance Minister Theo Waigel on Wednesday said the government might have to raise value added tax (VAT) and taxes on pensions in order to finance planned cuts of up to 30 billion marks ($19 billion) in income taxes.

Ahead of the yearly strategy meeting of his CSU party, Waigel rejected demands by coalition partner Free Democrats (FDP) to abolish the solidarity tax that has been at the centre of a coalition dispute.

The VAT hike, which many economists consider a near certainty, would be the government's last resort after first trying to plug gaps in financing by chopping billions in tax deductions for businesses and private individuals.
"If that is not sufficient, I would consider it legitimate to shift from direct to indirect taxes," Waigel said in an interview with the daily Sueddeutsche Zeitung newspaper.
"In many areas, we have the highest direct tax rates. We could achieve a reduction here and compensate it through our relatively low indirect tax rates, such as value added tax."

While declining to say which deductions would be targeted, Waigel said the government commission was scrutinising all exemptions and would "let the cat out of the bag" all at once after its final meeting on January 22.
"I can say one thing now: Most of them will be abolished or at least reduced," he said.
The main opposition Social Democrats (SPD) warned that the VAT hike was a veiled plan to introduce tax cuts for the wealthy and finance these with tax hikes for the middle class.

"The FDP, with its rock hard special interest policies for the wealthy and high-wage earners, will try everything to block any easing for normal wage earners," said SPD finance spokesman Joachim Poss.

Meanwhile ties between the conservative alliance of Chancellor Helmut Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU) and Waigel's CSU in the government coalition with the FDP remain strained because of a dispute over the unpopular solidarity tax.

Waigel lashed out again at the FDP, saying the tax -- a 7.5 percent income tax surcharge raised to aid eastern Germany -- brings in around 30 billion marks in revenue each year and could not be abolished without secure financing.
The centre-right coalition government agreed to cut the tax to 5.5 percent next year but the FDP is demanding it be scrapped completely around the turn of the century.
"No one so far has been able to show me how the federal government would be able to digest the loss of the solidarity tax all at once in the year 2000," Waigel said.

Prompted by the Federal Constitutional Court to eliminate unfairness towards civil servants in the taxation of pension payments, the government tax commission appears to have agreed on plans to raise the levy on pensions beginning in 1999.

Erwin Huber, Bavarian state finance minister, said the changes would probably not affect most pensioners, but only those with alternative sources of income, such as interest income or revenue from rented property. ($1=1.5711 Mark)
